**Saturday, June 23, 1956**

The summer of 1956 was when several large things happened at once — when the map of the world, the sound of popular music, the routes of American highways, and the architecture of the Cold War all shifted within weeks of each other. You were born at the center of it.

---

**Nasser confirmed as Egypt's president — exact date**

On the day you were born, Egyptians voted to confirm Gamal Abdel Nasser as their first president under a new constitution. The vote was the culminating moment of a sequence: ten days earlier, the last British troops had completed their withdrawal from the Suez Canal Zone; now Nasser held formal power over a country that had just reclaimed its own soil. One month later — July 26 — he nationalized the canal itself. The world you were born into and the Suez Crisis that autumn are separated by just over thirty days. You arrived at the exact pivot of that sequence, between the British leaving and Nasser reaching for the canal. The reshuffling of global power that followed — the humiliation of Britain and France, the confirmation of American and Soviet dominance, the acceleration of decolonization across the Arab world — all of it traced back to the weeks surrounding your birth.

---

**The Interstate Highway System — six days later**

On June 29, 1956 — six days after you were born — President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, authorizing the construction of 41,000 miles of interstate highways. It was the largest public works project in American history, inspired by the German Autobahn Eisenhower had studied during World War II and motivated equally by commerce and Cold War military logistics: a network wide enough and strong enough to move tanks if the Soviets invaded. The America you grew up in — its suburbs, its road trips, its drive-ins and truck stops and the particular restlessness of a country that could load into a car and go — was being legislated into existence the week of your birth. The landscape of your childhood was not yet built.

---

**Rock and roll as a declaration — the culture dividing**

By June 1956, rock and roll was no longer a novelty and not yet an institution. It was a confrontation. Elvis Presley's television appearances were drawing parental outrage and teenage devotion in roughly equal measure; Chuck Berry was writing songs about teenagers that teenagers recognized as true in ways their parents' music never had been; Little Richard was performing with an abandon that made adult authorities visibly uncomfortable. What was happening was not simply a new musical genre. It was a generation announcing — for the first time in American history with such force — that its sensibility was distinct from its parents', and that it intended to follow that sensibility wherever it led. The child born in June 1956 would come of age in the decade that announcement made possible.

---

**America's internal contradiction — the civil rights reckoning**

In June 1956, the United States was the world's leading democracy and maintained formal racial segregation across large parts of its territory. Schools, buses, lunch counters, drinking fountains — the apparatus of American apartheid was still legally intact. The Montgomery Bus Boycott was in its seventh month, the Supreme Court's ruling on school desegregation was two years old and being actively resisted across the South, and the Civil Rights Act that would begin to dismantle the legal structure was still eight years away. The person born on June 23, 1956 entered a country that had not yet decided — not legally, not culturally — whether all of its people were equal. They would spend their childhood watching that decision get forced.

---

**±30-day worldwide event: Britain completes its withdrawal from the Suez Canal Zone — June 13, 1956, ten days before your birth**

Ten days before you were born, the last British soldier departed the Suez Canal Zone, completing a withdrawal negotiated two years earlier under Egyptian pressure. For 74 years, British troops had occupied the canal — one of the most strategically vital waterways in the world. Their departure was a milestone in the long unwinding of the British Empire, and it was the direct precondition for what followed: a newly sovereign Nasser, emboldened by full control of his own country, nationalized the canal one month later. Britain and France went to war to take it back and were stopped — by American and Soviet pressure, simultaneously, for the first and only time in the Cold War. The empire that had dispatched troops to Suez in 1882 was over. It became undeniable ten days before you arrived.

---

**The lifetime that followed**

You are seventy years old. You were twelve during 1968 — the year that broke the optimism your generation had inherited. Thirteen when Armstrong walked on the Moon. Twenty when the Vietnam War ended, not in victory. Thirty-three when the Berlin Wall fell. Forty-five on September 11, 2001. Sixty-three when the pandemic began.

In seventy years: the contraceptive pill, the personal computer, satellite communication, the internet, the smartphone, the sequencing of the human genome, and now artificial intelligence. The child born on a Saturday in June 1956 arrived in a country whose highways were not yet built, whose racial laws had not yet fallen, whose music was in the middle of a revolution, and whose empire — the British one that had defined the previous century — was in the final stages of dissolving. The world that replaced all of that is the one you have been living in for decades.

---

**What kind of world did you enter?**

You were born at a genuine hinge — when the old arrangements were visibly ending and the new ones were not yet clear. The Suez Canal was about to change hands. The American interstate was about to be built. The music was already different. The racial order was beginning, slowly and at enormous cost, to crack. The seventy years that followed were not predictable from June 23, 1956 — but looking back, nearly everything that came was already in motion on the Saturday you were born.
